item.title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis for Graph Transformation Models with MolFoundry
item.description: arXiv:2610.20821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing-edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph-family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.
item.dc:creator: Marcel Friedrichs, Addie Jordon, Juri Kol\v{c}\'{a}k, Daniel Merkle

item.title: Reconstruction of continuous Archimedean t-norms from their section along an increasing curve
item.description: arXiv:2610.20874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The completion problem for continuous and Archimedean triangular norms (t-norms for short) consists in describing all the operators that take predefined values on a given subset of the unit square, and it reveals how much of a t-norm is determined by partial information. In this paper, we focus on the case where this subset is a parametric curve. We first formulate the problem in terms of the functional equation satisfied by an additive generator, and we then restrict our attention to curves of the form $(x,p(x))$ with $p$ continuous and increasing, which include the classical diagonal and horizontal section cases. We determine when the known values are compatible with a continuous and Archimedean t-norm, and we show that every completion is obtained by choosing the additive generator on a subinterval and reconstructing it elsewhere from the values on the curve. This description is recursive in general and becomes a closed formula under additional conditions, recovering the two classical results as particular cases. The completions are not unique, and we give examples with infinitely many t-norms sharing the same section along a curve. Finally, we combine our results with the reconstruction of a t-norm from its values above a level curve, which determines exactly the additive generator on that subinterval, so that the two pieces of information are complementary and together determine a unique completion.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Bauza-Llompart, Raquel Fernandez-Peralta, Marc Munar

item.title: Two Variables and Two-Dimensional Structures
item.description: arXiv:2610.20937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the two-variable fragment FO^2 of first-order logic over two-dimensional structures. Formulae may employ two linear orders <=_1, <=_2, their successor relations S_1, S_2, and auxiliary predicates of any arity. Despite two decades of work, three cases of finite satisfiability in this setting were still open; we settle all three. First, finite satisfiability of FO^2 with one linear order and one successor relation, of the same or of a different order, is NExpTime-complete, even with arbitrary auxiliary predicates and constant symbols. This closes a gap left open by Manuel and Zeume (CSL 2013). As an application, a reduction based on swaps of adjacent elements shows that order-invariance and order-successor-invariance of FO^2 are coNExpTime-complete. This reproves the main result of Zeume and Harwath (LICS 2016) and settles their question on order-successor-invariance. Second, finite satisfiability of FO^2 with two linear orders is ExpSpace-hard, already without auxiliary non-unary predicates, matching the upper bound known since 2010. Our reduction combines Kieronski's encoding of alternating Turing machines with the classical fact that the pre-order and post-order traversals of a tree define its descendant relation. Third, with two linear orders and the successor of one of them, finite satisfiability is in ExpSpace even with arbitrary auxiliary predicates, improving the previous 2NExpTime bound and confirming a conjecture of Zeume and Harwath. Together with known results, our theorems show that in two dimensions, auxiliary (non-unary) predicates and constants come for free: with or without them, the complexities coincide. All our proofs are simple.
item.dc:creator: Bartosz Jan Bednarczyk, Daumantas Kojelis, Krzysztof Szyma\'nski

item.title: Model Checking HyperRecHML is Decidable
item.description: arXiv:2610.21379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal hyperlogics combine explicit quantification over traces with temporal requirements evaluated over the quantified traces. HyperRecHML is a temporal hyperlogic which allows for arbitrary mixing of trace quantification and the use of fixed points for expressing temporal requirements, which makes it very expressive in comparison to other first-order hyperlogics. HyperRecHML has already been successfully applied in runtime verification, but the decidability of its model checking problem remains open. We answer this question positively by providing two main contributions. Firstly, a normalization procedure that allows to reduce arbitrary HyperRecHML formulas to a normal form with restricted nesting of trace quantification and fixed points. Secondly, we provide an automata-based model checking algorithm for formulas of this normal form. The complexity of our algorithm is comparable to similar ones for other hyperlogics, despite the extra expressive power.
item.dc:creator: Elli Anastasiadi, Kim Guldstrand Larsen, Martin Zimmermann

item.title: Anticipatory Commonsense with Moving Objects: An ASP-Based Framework for Predictive Reasoning with Interacting Trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2610.20867v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a general declarative framework for anticipatory reasoning about interactive motion in complex dynamic environments. Our focus is on (explainable) anticipatory space-time mental model formation at a semantic level to heuristically guide low-level motion computation. Our method is hybrid, modular and elaboration tolerant integrating: 1) An ASP model characterising the dynamics of interactive motion trajectories; 2) Semantically-guided prediction for deriving `branching trajectory futures'; and 3) An energy-based {optimisation} model to evaluate, rank and filter anticipations. We evaluate with the Argoverse 2 benchmark, where each anticipated trajectory carries an explicit, inspectable event-level hypothesis, unlike end-to-end stochastic prediction.
item.dc:creator: Julius Monsen, Jakob Suchan, Mehul Bhatt

item.title: Geometric Graph Representations via Compact SAT Encodings
item.description: arXiv:2610.22241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present compact SAT encodings and certifying exact solvers for boxicity and cubicity. The boxicity of a graph is the minimum dimension in which it is the intersection graph of axis-aligned boxes; cubicity is defined analogously using unit cubes. Grid-based formulations face a geometric discretization bottleneck, growing rapidly with the target dimension. We avoid this bottleneck by encoding the total order of interval endpoints in each coordinate. For an $n$-vertex graph and target dimension $d$, our boxicity encoding uses $O(n^2d)$ variables and $O(n^3d)$ clauses, both linear in $d$. Requiring the left- and right-endpoint orders to agree yields a cubicity encoding of the same asymptotic size. Satisfying models are decoded into independently checked geometric representations, while unsatisfiable instances used as lower-bound evidence carry mechanically verified DRAT certificates. In a controlled evaluation with 186 trials per encoding on standard and structured graph families, the order encoding solves 96.8% of trials, compared with 71.0% for the known grid formulation, and reduces mean PAR-2 time from 178.21 to 21.70 seconds. The pipeline also certifies exact values for several named graphs. We turn one such value into a reusable obstruction by proving that every Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ with $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$ contains an induced Desargues graph. The resulting lower bound, together with an explicit three-dimensional representation of $K(7,3)$, establishes $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(7,3))=3$. This disproves the conjecture of Caoduro and Sebo that $\operatorname{boxicity}(K(n,k))=n-k$ for all $k\ge3$ and $n\ge2k+1$.
item.dc:creator: L. Sunil Chandran, Rishikesh Gajjala, Suraj Kumar Sahoo, Aatman Supkar

item.title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22287v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.
item.dc:creator: Omar Adalat, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Francesco Belardinelli

item.title: Derivatives for Containers in Univalent Foundations
item.description: arXiv:2512.17484v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Containers conveniently represent a wide class of inductive data types. Their derivatives compute representations of types of one-hole contexts, useful for implementing tree-traversal algorithms. Derivatives of discrete containers (whose positions have decidable equality) satisfy a universal property with respect to linear morphisms of containers. This induces a well-behaved notion of linear substitution for one-hole contexts. Working in Univalent Foundations, we extend the derivative operation to untruncated containers (whose shapes and positions are arbitrary types). We prove that this derivative, defined in terms of a set of isolated positions, satisfies an appropriate universal property in the wild category of untruncated containers and linear morphisms, as well as basic laws with respect to constants, sums and products. A chain rule exists, but is in general non-invertible. In fact, a globally invertible chain rule is inconsistent in the presence of non-set types, and equivalent to a classical principle when restricted to set-truncated containers. We derive a rule for derivatives of least fixpoints from the chain rule, and characterize its invertibility. All of our results are formalized in Cubical Agda.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Joram, Niccol\`o Veltri

item.title: Proofs Without Nominals: G\"odel's Ontological Argument, its Shallow Embedding, and the Open Questions of the Monatshefte Notes
item.description: arXiv:2609.36279v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The shallow embedding of higher-order modal logic in classical higher-order logic, used in Benzm\"uller and Scott's Notes on G\"odel's and Scott's variants of the ontological argument, reaches beyond the modal object language: its quantifiers range over domains containing the nominals and satisfaction operators of hybrid logic. A proof using one proves a theorem of the embedding, not necessarily of the modal logic. Whether a result is one of the modal logic can be settled by replaying it in an explicit calculus, or, more cheaply and for all results at once, by analysing what the embedding's proofs substitute. Every statement the Notes prove has a proof in the embedding substituting nothing outside the object language, 294 of them explicit. The Notes' own proofs substitute none either; what it flags are terms a prover introduced. A soundness theorem over general models closed under the object language, and a sentence of that language the embedding proves but which fails in one of them, fix what the certificate says. The Notes' three open questions are settled too, without nominals, but by the empty instance of the conjunction axiom, too cheaply to convince. Generalised to G\"odel's "any number of summands", the axiom covers the empty conjunction and the singleton. This article restricts it to at least two different conjuncts, a non-degenerate reading of G\"odel's footnote, and settles them again without nominals. In effect only the empty conjunction is excluded; the singleton comes back with the other axioms. In one variant the restriction refutes the possible existence of a God-like being; the answers return, with no side condition, once the Notes' non-emptiness clause is confined to G\"odel's essence. Every theorem here is verified in Isabelle/HOL and independently in Lean 4, the separating model in its propositional part; the countermodels are Nitpick's, checked by the build.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Benzm\"uller

item.title: Fixed-Point Scaffolding in the Clef Programming Language
item.description: arXiv:2606.02854v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Native compilation changes how a program represents values and performs operations from processor to processor. In our view, proofs that justify source-level decisions must remain connected to those changes. We develop fixed-point scaffolding for this continuity in Clef and our Composer compiler. Our Program Semantic Graph retains types, joint constraints and proof dependencies. A thin MLIR middle end witnesses their settled consequences for native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA realization. The account connects nanopass traversal with preservation contracts, structural theorems and adjoint interfaces between reasoning modes. Four verification tiers organize automatic inference and reusable domain and system proofs, with probabilistic relations admitted at Tier 4. Established lower-tier facts can directly support richer derivations. We state conditions for composing lowering contracts and assembling compatible program segments, then show how their dependencies govern differential compilation after an edit. A worked foreign-call boundary follows source ranges through argument marshaling, the actual call and return conversion. Current FFI mechanisms bind checking evidence to those witnessed operations. A recent paper from Urschel provides elimination-growth bounds that supply a quantitative example. Reusable premises inform representation and error contracts that retain their sampling, arithmetic and exceptional-path assumptions. A further example admits value-indexed pairing through ordinary MLIR operations, connecting this scaffold to negative and fractional types. Together these constructions explain how a thin middle end can carry the consequences of rich source proofs into unboxed computation graphs. Integrity and efficiency share the same retained evidence. It justifies native realizations and identifies which analyses, proofs and lowered fragments remain reusable during development.
item.dc:creator: Houston Haynes

item.title: Neuro-Relational Programs: Unifying Queries and Neural Computation over Structured Data
item.description: arXiv:2606.11946v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The conventional approach to deep learning over relational databases applies neural models, such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), to a graph representation of the database. Recent approaches instead operate on databases directly, associating tuples with embeddings and extending query mechanisms to jointly process embeddings and relational content. Inspired by these developments, we introduce Neuro-Relational Programs (NRPs), a declarative query language for relational databases whose facts carry numeric vector embeddings. NRPs extend Datalog-style rules with operations that combine, aggregate, and transform embeddings, thereby interleaving relational reasoning and learnable neural components within a single formalism. This yields a general approach to neural computation over relational data: an NRP can be read both as a query plan with trainable components and as a neural architecture with relational structure built in. Natural syntactic fragments of NRPs recover existing architectures and query formalisms. Zero-ary NRPs correspond to non-adaptive query algorithms; monadic NRPs generalize GNN-style message passing and precisely capture Deep Homomorphism Networks, a connection that we extend to frontier-guarded NRPs over databases with row-ids. We characterize the expressive power of unrestricted NRPs with ReLU-FFN transformations by FOCQ, an extension of first-order logic with counting interpreted over real-weighted structures, yielding a precise connection with uniform TC$^0$ over ordered databases. Together, these results establish NRPs as a broad declarative framework for querying and neural computation over relational data.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proc. ACM Manag. Data 4(5) (PODS), Article 300, November 2026
item.dc:creator: Arie Soeteman, Balder ten Cate, Maurice Funk, Benny Kimelfeld, Carsten Lutz, Moritz Sch\"onherr

item.title: Bidirectional Elaborators \`a la Carte
item.description: arXiv:2607.09564v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines. We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-L\"of type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-L\"of type theory.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Slattery, Jonathan Sterling

item.title: Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.07226v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.
item.dc:creator: T. Y. Tsui, Zihao Ye, Pengxiang Cai, Yanchao Li, Yuqiang Li, Zhehong Ai

item.title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
item.description: arXiv:2610.12911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.
item.dc:creator: Houston Haynes
